## Trend and time series data

> A **time series** is a sequence of data points indexed, listed, or graphed in chronological order. --- Wikipedia

<br>

Main topic

* **Time series analysis**

  * What already happened?

  * Extract meaningful statistics and other characteristics of the data
  
. . .

* **Time series forecasting**

  * What will happen in the future?

  * Predict future values based on previously observed values


## Longitudinal data and time series structure

* Consider a *single observation* measured across time

* Time series data usually has the following structure:

| Variable   | $T_1$    | $T_2$    | $\dots$  | $T_J$    |
| ---------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- |
| $X_1$      | $x_{11}$ | $x_{12}$ | $\dots$  | $x_{1J}$ |
| $X_2$      | $x_{21}$ | $x_{22}$ | $\dots$  | $x_{2J}$ |
| $\vdots$   | $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ | $\dots$  | $\vdots$ |
| $X_P$      | $x_{P1}$ | $x_{P2}$ | $\dots$  | $x_{PJ}$ |

* With $N$ observations, there are $N$ of these matrices

* Time may consist of regularly- or irregularly-spaced intervals

## Time series plot

Scatterplot with `n_phds` on the y-axis and `year` on the x-axis + Add line to emphasize order + Manually set x-axis breaks to show every year

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-width: 12
stats_phd_year |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = n_phds)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = unique(stats_phd_year$year),
                     labels = unique(stats_phd_year$year))
```

## Drop points to emphasize trend

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-width: 12
stats_phd_year |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = n_phds)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = unique(stats_phd_year$year),
                     labels = unique(stats_phd_year$year))
```

## Fill area under the line

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-width: 12
stats_phd_year |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = n_phds)) +
  geom_area(fill = "cyan") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = unique(stats_phd_year$year),
                     labels = unique(stats_phd_year$year))
```

## Plotting multiple time series: use lines with colors

```{r}

```

```{r}

#| fig-height: 6.5
```

Also known as a spaghetti plot
:::

## Highlight specific lines

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-width: 12
stats_phd |> 
  filter(!(field %in% c("Biometrics and biostatistics", "Statistics (mathematics)"))) |> 
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(x = year, y = n_phds, group = field),
            color = "gray", linewidth = 1, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = filter(stats_phd, field %in% c("Biometrics and biostatistics", "Statistics (mathematics)")),
            aes(x = year, y = n_phds, color = field),
            linewidth = 1.5, alpha = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = unique(stats_phd$year),
                     labels = unique(stats_phd$year))
```

## Characteristics of time series

* **Trends**: Does the variable increase or decrease over time, on average?

* **Seasonality**: Are there changes in the variable that regularly happen (e.g., every winter, every hour, etc.)?

* **Noise**: Variation in the variable beyond average trends and seasonality

## Moving average

* Moving/rolling averages are a starting point for visualizing how a trend changes over time

* Intuition

  * Divide the data into small subsets ("windows")

  * Compute the average within each window

  * Connect the averages together to make a trend line

* This is sometimes called a simple moving average

* Have we seen this before?

## Computing a moving average

Formally, a moving average can be written as

$$\mu_k = \frac{1}{h}\sum_{t=k - h + 1}^k X_t$$

* Large $h$: smooth line; captures global trends

* Small $h$: jagged/volatile line; captures local trends

## Time series visualization example

Data: Mauna Loa monthly atmospheric  $\text{CO}_2$ concentration 1959 to 1997

```{r}
#| echo: false
# co2_tbl |> 
#   write_csv("data/co2.csv")
```

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
co2 <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/qntkhvn/36-315-summer26/refs/heads/master/data/co2.csv")
co2 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = obs_date, y = co2_val)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Time index", y = "CO2 (ppm)")
```

## Use [`ggseas`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ggseas/vignettes/ggseas.html) package to plot moving averages

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
library(ggseas)
co2 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = obs_date, y = co2_val)) + 
  geom_line(color = "red") +
  stat_rollapplyr(width = 12, align = "right") +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "CO2 (ppm)", title = "Width = 12")
```

## Moving window

* Setting `width = 12` and `align = "right"` means for each point, plot the average of a **moving window** consisting of that point and the 11 points behind it 

  * Since this is monthly data, this is the average of a year’s worth of data
  
  * Note that there is no trend line for the first 11 points on the left-hand side of the graph
  
* Choose a `width` value that is "just right" 

  * Want the trend to be smooth enough, but also don’t want to deviate from the data too much
  
## Moving window

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(patchwork)
wid2 <- co2 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = obs_date, y = co2_val)) +
  geom_line(color = "red") +
  stat_rollapplyr(width = 2, align = "right") +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "CO2 (ppm)",
       title = "Width = 2")

wid24 <- co2 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = obs_date, y = co2_val)) +
  geom_line(color = "red") +
  stat_rollapplyr(width = 24, align = "right") +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "CO2 (ppm)",
       title = "Width = 24")
wid2 + wid24
```


## Other moving averages

* **Cumulative moving average**: The average at time $k$ is the average of all points at and before $k$. Mathematically:

$$\mu_k^{\textsf{(CMA)}} = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{t=1}^k X_t$$

. . .

* **Weighted moving average**: Same as simple moving average, but different measurements get different weights for the average.

$$\mu_k^{\textsf{(WMA)}} = \frac{\sum_{t=k - h + 1}^k X_t \cdot w_t}{ \sum_{t=k - h + 1}^k w_t}$$


## Lags

* Time series data are not independent and identically distributed (iid)

  * Example: today's temperature is correlated with yesterday's temperature

. . .

* **Lags**: a time offset used to compare observations separated by a fixed number of time steps

  * Lag 1: compare $X_t$ with $X_{t - 1}$

  * Lag 2: compare $X_t$ with $X_{t - 2}$

  * and so on...

. . .

* Given time measurements $(X_1, X_2, X_3, X_4, X_5)$

  * Lag 1 compares $(X_2, X_3, X_4, X_5)$ with $(X_1, X_2, X_3, X_4)$

  * Lag 2 compares $(X_3, X_4, X_5)$ vs $(X_1, X_2, X_3)$.


## Autocorrelation

* **Autocorrelation**: correlation between a time series and a lagged version of itself

. . .

* Define $r_{\ell}$ as the correlation between a time series and lag $\ell$ of that time series

  * Lag 1: $r_1$ is correlation between $(X_2, X_3, X_4, X_5)$ and $(X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4)$

  * Lag 2: $r_2$ is correlation between $(X_3, X_4, X_5)$ and $(X_1,X_2,X_3)$

  * and so on...

. . .

* Common diagnostic: plot $\ell$ on x-axis, $r_{\ell}$ on y-axis

  * Reveals if correlations are significantly large/small for certain lags


## Autocorrelation plots

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
library(ggfortify)
auto_corr <- acf(co2$co2_val, plot = FALSE)
autoplot(auto_corr)
```


## Autocorrelation plots and seasonality

* With strong global trends, autocorrelations will be very positive

* Visualize autocorrelations after removing the global trend

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
wid12 <- co2 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = obs_date, y = co2_val)) +
  geom_line(color="red") +
  stat_rollapplyr(width = 12, align = "right") +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "CO2 (ppm)")

co2 <- co2 |>
  mutate(moving_avg = zoo::rollapply(co2_val, width = 12, FUN = "mean", align = "right", fill = NA),
         resid = co2_val - moving_avg)

resid_plot <- co2 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = obs_date, y = resid)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Residuals of CO2 (ppm)")

library(patchwork)
wid12 + resid_plot
```

## Autocorrelation plots and seasonality

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
# ACF of the residuals (except the first 11 points, which are NA)
autoplot(acf(tail(co2$resid, -11), plot = FALSE))
```

## Seasonal decomposition

* STL decomposition (**S**easonal decomposition of **T**ime series by **L**oess)

* Break down a time series into three characteristics: **trend**, **seasonality**, **noise**

. . .

* Use `ggsdc()` (from [`ggseas`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ggseas/vignettes/ggseas.html)) to visualize seasonal decomposition

  * `observed`: original time series

  * `trend`: loess curve; global trend

  * `seasonality`: another loess curve as the seasonality (observed - trend) 

  * `irregular`:  irregular/residual noise (observed - trend - seasonality)
  
  * In other words: `trend` + `seasonality` + `irregular` = `observed`

## Seasonal decomposition

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-width: 6
co2 |>
  ggsdc(aes(obs_date, co2_val), frequency = 12, method = "stl", s.window = 12) +
  geom_line() + 
  labs(x = "Year", y = "CO2 (ppm)")
```
